newsitem.title: USA: Gold supply seen weighing on demand - JP Morgan.
newsitem.headline: Gold supply seen weighing on demand - JP Morgan.

text.p: Rising gold mine output in the next ten years may be sufficient to meet demand, limiting the upside for gold prices, JP Morgan vice president for commodities, Kevin Crisp, said Monday.
"I think demand is going to be met in the future by more than adequate levels of supply," Crisp told the annual conference of the Gold and Silver Institute.
Crisp showed the conference a chart projecting gold prices in a $3.30-$3.80 an ounce range, out to the year 2005.

"Clearly, gold prices will trade over a wider range during the period, but the key point is that the price of gold may well trade in defined ranges for prolonged periods of time over the next ten years," he said.
Gold mine output was forecast to rise to 2,700-2,900 tonnes by 2005, from 2,600-2,800 tonnes in 2000, and 2,328 tonnes in 1996 and 2,135 tonnes in 1990, Crisp said.
Total supply, including scrap, was forecast to rise to 3,950-4,550 tonnes in 2005, from 3,800-4,400 tonnes in 2000 and 3,431 tonnes in 1996 and 3,093 tonnes in 1990.

The largest expansions in gold mining are set to come from emerging markets, as exploration spending translates into new deposits in Latin America, Africa and Southeast Asia, while South African output will stabilize around the 500-tonne-a-year level, he said.

"Rising exploration spending, more overseas spending on exploration, increasingly freer markets, and improved or new funding and risk-management structures strongly support our outlook for mine supply," he said.
"If my supply-side forecasts are realized, the burdens placed upon demand, and particularly the jewelry sector, are going to grow substantially," he said.

Goldfields Mineral Services Limited's annual survey showed world gold jewelry fabrication rose 28 percent between 1990 and 1996, and last year the jewelry industry consumed 460 tonnes more gold than was produced by the world's mines.

"There is therefore scope for rising mine output to be absorbed by consumers as long as other sources of supply are maintained at levels not far different from those seen on average in recent years," Crisp said.
"Demand growth to be maintained will require greater innovation in product development to meet changes in consumer tastes and to compete for discretionary spending."
